title: The long conversation of stone
paragraphs: The Korean Peninsula contains rocks with very different origins and ages. Some record the remains of ancient continental crust; others were produced as sediments accumulated, buried materials metamorphosed, or molten rock cooled into solid masses. This variety tells a story not of one dramatic birth but of repeated episodes of formation and transformation. A landscape that appears continuous to a traveler may be a mosaic of geological histories stitched together over immense spans of time.

Tectonic forces help explain why rock bodies are folded, fractured, intruded, or tilted. Erosion then reshapes the result. A mountain range is not simply something that rose once and remained unchanged. Its surface is continuously affected by rain, frost, rivers, vegetation, slope movement, and changes in climate. Even when geological motion becomes comparatively quiet, the landscape continues to evolve. Valleys widen, sediment moves downstream, and coastlines receive the material worn away from distant highlands.

These processes created the underlying materials of later human life. Stone supplied raw material for tools, bedrock helped determine relief, and weathering contributed to soils with different characteristics. Rivers connected uplands to lowlands. The history of land therefore flows into the history of resources, livelihoods, settlement, and technology, although the human uses of these environments came vastly later.
